questions.q: What does DeepAR output at each forecast step?
why: That would be a point forecast model.
Correct: for example mu and sigma.

questions.q: Which distribution does the DeepAR paper suggest for counts of items sold?
why: A normal allows negative values and fits counts poorly.
A uniform is not a good fit for demand.

questions.q: y = 5, mu = 5, sigma = 2. Gaussian NLL = 0.5·log(2π·σ²) + (y − μ)²/(2σ²). Round to 3 decimals.
Why does NLL include the log(sigma) term?
options: To stop the model from choosing a huge sigma to hide all errors.
why: Correct: without it, a large sigma would make the error term tiny.

questions.q: At forecast time, how do you get a 90% prediction interval from DeepAR?
options: Add and subtract 1.64 from the mean.
Sample many paths, then take the 5% and 95% quantiles at each step.
Train a second model on the errors.
why: That is only right for a normal with sigma 1 and no feedback; sampling captures growth in uncertainty.
Not needed; the samples already give it.

questions.q: Your DeepAR 80% intervals contain only 60% of the real values on test data. What do you do?
options: Treat it as overconfident: check the distribution choice, scaling, data shift and consider calibration (for example conformal).
why: Coverage far below 80% is a failure.

questions.q: What is teacher forcing, and what is the risk?
options: Feed real values in training; at test time, the model uses its own guesses and errors can build up.
Use a teacher model for labels; no risk.
Force the model to use all features; risk of overfitting.
why: That is distillation, not teacher forcing.
